rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window and reduce risk of missing strongly retained compounds. This gives a useful first map of retention distribution and whether early peaks are unretained or late peaks still require stronger conditions.

All 10 compounds eluted well within the broad gradient, so trim the gradient window to the actual elution window to keep all peaks inside the gradient and reduce time penalty. This should maintain strong resolution while shortening the run and revealing whether the critical mid-cluster improves under a narrower, shallower effective window.

The narrowed window was too weak and pushed the last compound into a long high-retention tail, so return to the strong full-range gradient and now test slope sensitivity by halving tG. Comparing this to injection 1 will show whether the critical 6–7 region improves with a shallower or steeper gradient while likely reducing run time.

The comparison of 10 versus 20 min shows the critical mid-cluster loses resolution when the gradient is made steeper, so move back toward a shallower slope while keeping run time shorter than injection 1. This should test whether the best CRF sits near the shortest tG that still restores full resolution in the 5–7 region.

The critical pair improves strongly as the gradient is made shallower, and 14 min is close to optimal already, so test a small increase in tG to see if the 6–7 pair clears 1.5 while still avoiding any time penalty. This is the most direct refinement around the current best method.

Since the 6–7 pair responds to slope but 16 min paid a small time penalty, keep the near-optimal 14 min gradient and use temperature to tune selectivity. A 5 C drop may improve the close mid-cluster enough to preserve zero time penalty while lifting the current limiting pair.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by collapsing a different pair, so test the opposite direction at the otherwise best slope. A 5 C increase may reorder or spread the critical mid-cluster while likely keeping the run within the no-penalty time region.

Temperature perturbations both hurt, so keep T at 40 C and refine only gradient slope around the optimum. Testing 12 min brackets the best region from the fast side and will clarify whether 14 min is truly optimal or if a slightly shorter gradient can preserve resolution with the same zero time penalty.

The 12–16 min series indicates the limiting pair improves monotonically with shallower gradient, but 16 min just began to incur a time penalty. Testing 18 min will show whether the resolution gain is large enough to outweigh added time, helping define whether 14 or 16 min is the true optimum.

The best region is clearly near 14 min at 40 C, so now trim only the high-end organic limit slightly while keeping the successful slope regime. The last peak is far from the end of the gradient, so a modestly lower phi1 may improve selectivity in the mid-cluster without causing late hold elution or a time penalty.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved CRF while preserving full elution and zero time penalty, so continue trimming the high-end organic limit in small steps. This directly tests whether a slightly narrower, shallower gradient further improves the persistent 6–7 selectivity without pushing the last peak too late.

The best chemistry so far is the trimmed upper window at phi1 0.90, and 14 min gave the top CRF, so now test whether a slightly steeper version preserves the improved selectivity while gaining margin on run time. This will tell us whether the phi1 improvement shifts the tG optimum shorter than before.

At phi1 0.90, the 12 min gradient was too steep, so test the shallower side of the local optimum. This should show whether the improved phi window allows better resolution than the current best while keeping the run time low enough to avoid much penalty.

The best method is now clearly phi1 0.90 at 14 min, and the remaining limitation is a single close mid-cluster pair, so revisit temperature with the improved phi window. A lower temperature may alter selectivity differently here than it did at phi1 0.95 and could lift the limiting pair without adding a time penalty.

Lowering temperature again hurt selectivity, so test the opposite direction at the current best phi window to complete the local temperature map. If 45 C also worsens the same cluster, that will confirm 40 C is the true optimum and let us focus remaining injections on finer phi-window tuning.

Temperature is clearly inferior to 40 C, so return to the best conditions and now test the low-end gradient bound. Raising phi0 slightly may reposition the crowded mid-elution cluster within the gradient and improve the limiting pair while still keeping the first peak well retained.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved the best CRF, so continue in the same direction to see if the crowded cluster benefits further from a slightly stronger starting composition. The first peak is still retained enough that there is room to test a higher phi0 without risking an unretained front.

The best point is at phi0 0.10, and raising phi0 further did not help, so now combine the improved low-end bound with the previously favorable trimmed high-end bound. This narrower window should modestly shallow the effective gradient around the crowded cluster and could convert the remaining near-threshold pair into the top CRF.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so this injection should probe robustness around the optimum rather than chase a higher impossible score. Testing a slightly higher phi0 with the winning phi1 checks whether the optimum sits on a broad plateau or whether 0.10/0.85 is uniquely best.

With two neighboring methods now at the maximum score, map the lower-phi1 edge of the optimum plateau. Reducing phi1 one more step tests whether the upper bound can be tightened further while preserving full gradient elution and perfect CRF.

Lowering phi1 to 0.80 was too aggressive, so stay at the successful phi1 0.85 and now define the upper phi0 edge of the optimum region. This checks whether the perfect-score plateau extends to a stronger start or if early peaks begin to approach the unretained zone.

Now that the phi-window optimum is clear, test whether the perfect-score plateau also extends to a slightly shorter gradient under the winning window. If CRF stays at 1.000, this would reveal a faster equally optimal method; if not, it confirms 14 min as the true tG optimum.

Since phi0 0.15 also gave a perfect score at 14 min, test whether the slightly stronger start can support a shorter 12 min gradient under the same successful window. This maps whether the maximum-score plateau extends diagonally in phi0–tG space.

The remaining unknown around the optimum plateau is the shallower-gradient side under the winning phi window. Testing 16 min confirms whether the perfect score is robust to extra resolution gain or whether 14 min is the unique balance point before time penalty dominates.

For the final injection, map the last nearby untested point around the two winning methods to complete the local landscape. This checks whether the perfect-score plateau extends to a shallower gradient when combined with the stronger start, even though the current evidence suggests 14 min is optimal.
